summary: Describes S-CUSP, a simple protocol developed by China Mobile, Huawei and ZTE for control and user plane separation of a Broadband Network Gateway (BNG). It carries communication between the control plane and the user plane in a fixed access network.

eli5.summary: A busy post office splits the people who decide where mail goes from the people who carry it. This is how those two groups talk.

questions: how are bng control and user planes separated
what is carrier-grade nat in s-cusp
how does s-cusp handle subscriber sessions
subtitle: Protocol for splitting BNG control and forwarding functions into separate planes.

tldr.problem: Traditional broadband network gateways (BNGs) mix user management (authentication, policy) and traffic forwarding in one device, making it hard to scale, update policy globally, or optimize each function separately.
tldr.mechanism: S-CUSP defines a protocol for communication between a centralized Control Plane (CP, user management) and distributed User Planes (UP, forwarding). The CP sends session states and routes to UPs via TLV-formatted messages over a control channel. UPs report session events and status back to the CP.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now centralize user management and distribute traffic forwarding, improving flexibility, redundancy, and resource utilization.

facts.label: Use cases
facts.value: IPoE, PPPoE, L2TP, WLAN, CGN, L3 leased line

today: RFC 8772 is an Informational RFC, not an IETF standard. S-CUSP was designed by China Mobile, Huawei, and ZTE and is in production use by these operators. It is not part of the broader IETF standards track and is presented in this RFC to make it available to the industry for interoperability and reference.

sections.title: The Split Broadband Gateway
sections.content:
A Broadband Network Gateway (BNG) is an edge router that connects residential and small-business subscribers to the Internet. It handles two distinct functions: (1) subscriber access control—authenticating users, assigning addresses, enforcing policies, managing sessions; and (2) traffic forwarding—routing packets to the network, enforcing QoS, collecting statistics.

Traditionally, these functions are tightly coupled in one device. This creates problems: the CP and forwarding plane interfere with each other, scaling is limited, global policy changes require updates to many devices, and resources cannot be optimized independently. S-CUSP enables Control and User Plane Separation (CUPS): a centralized CP handles user management for multiple distributed UPs that handle forwarding. The CP can be virtualized and run as VNFs. UPs can be simple forwarding engines spread across the network.

This is described in a Broadband Forum technical report (TR-384) and is in use by operators including China Mobile, Huawei, and ZTE.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big post office, the control side (deciding routes and rules) moves to a central office, while mail carriers (routers) stay distributed. S-CUSP is how they coordinate.

sections.title: Control Plane and User Plane Architecture
sections.content:
The Control Plane (CP) runs the following functions: address management (unified address pools, carrier-grade NAT), AAA (authentication with RADIUS/Diameter), subscriber management (session state, forwarding policies), access management (PPPoE, DHCP, L2TP processing), and UP management (health monitoring, channel maintenance).

The User Plane (UP) runs: routing control (instantiating routing, multicast, MPLS), forwarding plane (traffic forwarding, QoS, statistics), and subscriber detection (monitoring if a subscriber is still online).

Three interfaces connect them. The Service Interface (Si) relays dial-up control packets (PPPoE, DHCP, L2TP) between CP and UP using VXLAN tunnels. The Control Interface (Ci) carries the S-CUSP protocol—messages for session management, routing updates, and resource reports. The Management Interface (Mi) uses NETCONF to configure the links and templates.

The separation allows the CP to be centralized (even virtualized), while UPs are distributed. A single CP manages multiple UPs, and multiple CPs can manage one UP for redundancy.
sections.eli5: The control plane is the central office. User planes are branch offices. Three channels let them talk: one for mail-forwarding setup, one for session commands, one for configuration.

sections.title: Subscriber Session Management
sections.content:
When a subscriber (residential user) connects, the following happens. The UP receives access packets (dial-up request over PPPoE or DHCP) and relays them to the CP via the Si channel using VXLAN. The CP authenticates the subscriber via AAA, assigns an IP address, and creates a session entry. The CP then sends a Create Subscriber Session message to the UP on the Ci channel, listing the session ID, subscriber MAC, IP address, and any subscriber-specific policies. The UP installs forwarding entries for that subscriber and begins forwarding its traffic.

During the session, the CP can send Update Subscriber Session messages to change policies (QoS, bandwidth limits) or add new parameters like NAT bindings for carrier-grade NAT. The UP applies these changes immediately. When the subscriber goes offline, the CP sends a Delete Subscriber Session message, and the UP removes the forwarding entries and resources.

The UP also reports events to the CP: statistics (bytes sent/received), detection results (subscriber still online or gone), and status changes. This allows the CP to monitor and troubleshoot.
sections.eli5: CP: "I authenticated Alice on MAC 001. Give her IP 192.0.2.10 and limit her to 10 Mbps." UP: "Got it, I'm routing her traffic." Later: "Alice is offline now." CP: "Delete her session."

sections.title: S-CUSP Messages and TLVs
sections.content:
S-CUSP messages are binary-formatted. A common header identifies the message type and length. Messages are sent over TCP/UDP on a configured port. There are several message categories:

Control messages: Hello (handshake), Keepalive (heartbeat), Sync_Request/Sync_Begin/Sync_Data/Sync_End (data synchronization after connection), Update_Request/Update_Response (subscriber session changes).

Event messages: The UP reports subscriber statistics or detection results.

Report messages: The UP reports device status (board and interface status).

CGN messages: For carrier-grade NAT, messages to request, renew, and release public IP address pools and port ranges.

Each message contains Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. For example, a Basic Subscriber TLV holds the MAC address, subscriber name, and access type. An IPv4 Subscriber TLV adds the IP address and VLAN. Optional sub-TLVs carry CAR (Committed Access Rate) for QoS, interface descriptions, policy details, and vendor-specific extensions.
sections.eli5: Messages are tagged boxes of information. A message might say "Session Update" (the tag), here are the new QoS limits (the contents).

sections.title: Supported Access Methods
sections.content:
S-CUSP supports multiple subscriber access methods. IPoE (IP over Ethernet): Subscribers connect directly, get IP via DHCP (v4 or v6) or IPv6 autoconfiguration. PPPoE (PPP over Ethernet): Subscribers dial in, authenticate via PPP, then get IP. L2TP: Subscribers use L2TP tunnels to a concentrator (LAC) or network server (LNS), often for VPN. WLAN: Subscribers connect via wireless access points. L3 Leased Line: Permanent, static connections. CGN (Carrier-Grade NAT): Many subscribers share a pool of public addresses; the BNG translates private addresses to public and back.

For each access method, the RFC describes the CP and UP message flow: how the subscription is created, authenticated, assigned an address, and routed. The flows differ slightly because PPPoE and L2TP require PPP authentication while IPoE relies on DHCP.
sections.eli5: Different ways to plug in: Ethernet with DHCP, dial-up PPP, VPN tunnels, wireless, or static line. Each has its own flow, but S-CUSP handles all of them.

sections.title: Session Reliability and Synchronization
sections.content:
S-CUSP must be reliable because a lost session message means a subscriber loses connectivity or the CP loses visibility. To ensure reliability, sessions are synchronized when a CP-UP connection is established or restored. After a Hello handshake, the CP sends a Sync_Request to the UP. The UP responds with Sync_Begin, then streams all its current sessions in Sync_Data messages, then sends Sync_End. The CP merges this state with its own database, resolving any discrepancies (e.g., a session the CP thinks is active but the UP has already deleted).

A Keepalive timer ensures both sides know the connection is alive. If no messages arrive within the dead timer interval, the connection is torn down and a new one is established, triggering a new synchronization. This allows a failed CP to be replaced and a failed UP to rejoin the network without orphaned sessions.

Vendor extensions (vendor-specific messages and sub-TLVs) allow operators to add proprietary features without breaking interoperability.
sections.eli5: When control and forwarding reconnect, they compare notes: "Here's what I think is happening." "Here's what I have." They resolve disagreements and move on. If neither hears from the other, they break up and reconnect fresh.
